full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll tell you a bit about what we're doing to being with. We're interviewing female students about their educational experiences and their experiences of the workplace as well. We've mainly been interviewing placement students before they go on placement and then again when they're on the placement, but we've had a few problems trying to find people who are actually going on a placement so we're trying to.

Subject:	Yeah, a lot of people have had trouble this year so…

Interviewer:	So we've decided to include the Network 75 people on it as well, so some of the things might not go quite as smoothly, so if there's anything that doesn't make sense, just say – that's fine. Is it mechanical engineering that you're doing?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you do 'A' levels?

Subject:	Yeah I did. I did Economics and Technology, because I wasn't really fussed on the Physics and Maths but I wish I had done it now because I had to do a foundation year then last year, to be able to go through to the degree and I wish I had done Physics for 'A' level now, it would have made things a lot easier.

Interviewer:	OK what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	I went to a Catholic secondary school and I went to a Catholic primary school as well, so overall I think – I mean there's a lot of schools who offer like media studies and general studies and things like that. We didn't have anything like that. The basic options we had, for 'A' levels – the only thing other than regular subjects for GCSE was Economics and Sociology and that was about it really.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got any previous work experience at all?

Subject:	I did 3 weeks work experience. I've been [company] in [town], which is aircraft servicing, and that was really good. I really wanted to work there. I couldn't wait to finish school and just go and work there because I thought it would be so easy- huh, but it's not.

Interviewer:	OK. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, when and why do you think you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	I really don't know. Loads of people ask me and I let – they say when did you decide you liked it – and I just say, I don't know. Because I can't actually remember sitting down and thinking, oh I wouldn't mind doing that. (Yeah) But I can't remember when and I can't remember why. I just got into it – I just did, that's all. It's a bit different I think and not what people expect of a little girl.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what do you think it is that appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	I don't know. I think it is because it's – for a girl it's very different and I think there's always something different you know, like there's never two days the same or anything like that. I think it's just challenging all the time, I think that's why I'm enjoying it, because I don't get bored.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do any careers research or did you know any engineers to talk to or anything like that?

Subject:	My step-dad was –worked at [company] and his brother, but other than that I didn't really know anyone and I sort of spoke to them and I think it was because they (?) so exciting, because they were on the engine of a plane, and I think I just got excited about that. (Yeah) But other than that I didn't really know anyone or do any research. I sort of researched into apprenticeships in the Army and Corus and things like that, but other than that I never really looked into it that much, I just thought yeah, I want to do that, I'll have a go at that.

Interviewer:	OK, what made you decide to come to University instead of doing an apprenticeship or something?

Subject:	Erm, well I signed for – I tried for my apprenticeship when I was 16, because I didn't want to go back to school and do 'A' levels, and I got offered a few, but in the end I had quite good results in my GSCE's and my mother was like ah, it's gonna be a waste if you don't go back. So I went back and then I still wasn't going to come and I thought oh well, I may as well do it. I'm not ready for the big, wide world yet, so I just sort of – picked a couple of local Uni's and applied to them, and came down here with a friend and I really liked it down here, so, I just thought yeah, go on then, you can do that for a couple of years.

Interviewer:	OK, what appealed to you about doing the Network 75 programme?

Subject:	I think it was – I can remember last year struggling for money a bit. I thought the money would be handy, plus I'd have 5 years experience that someone sitting next to me in my exam might never get (yeah) and I just thought it would be different – it's not just sitting in a Uni doing nothing (yeah) and I just thought, yeah, the experience is going to be handy, because even if I don't necessarily get on with that company, I've still got the experience – they've taught me to move somewhere better, or bigger or whatever.

Interviewer:	Yeah, are you enjoying it so far?

Subject:	Yeah, they're really good.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider going to another University or studying full-time then?

Subject:	Erm, the only other Uni's I really applied to was like [university 1] – two in [university 2], and [university 3] and [university 3] rejected me. I didn't like [university 1] and I wasn't that keen on – I liked [university 1] but I wasn't as keen on [university 1] as I was on coming here because I just thought, ah, it's closer – like if something goes wrong (yeah) but it's far enough that I could be on my own and grow up a bit.

Interviewer:	Yeah, did you do your foundation here as well?

Subject:	Yeah, 

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that if the Network 75 thing hadn't been available you'd have done the course full time or…?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely I would have done it full time. Yeah, I think I definitely would have – I wouldn't have gone and looked for someone to employ me while I was work – er, studying. I don't think I even would have done a sandwich year or anything like that, so yeah, I probably would have just got my head down and done it.

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided to do engineering, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	I did, but I didn't realise how some people would react to it. Like, I've gone out on site, with the company I work for now (yeah) and even if I walk up to a gatehouse first, and there's a man behind me, they'll look over my head and talk to the man behind me (really?). And I didn't realise people will – I thought people would be encouraging but some people really put you down (yeah) and the way they act – they act totally different when I'm sitting in the canteen talking to them, than when I'm not. And I just think well why? There's nothing – it's not like the old days now. But I realised it was quite male dominated, it was just the way people reacted to it that scared me more than anything (yeah). I can remember going for my interview in [university 2], and they split you up from your parents and you've go on a bus and you have a tour and everything and I was on a bus – a 52 seater bus, with 40 other boys and not one person spoke to me, and I thought oh great, I've got this for the next 3 to 4 years. But I've just got used to it now and I think I've sort of – it's built my confidence to a certain extent because I'll just start talking to people whether they want to or not. Whether they're scared of me or not, I'll just start talking to them.

Interviewer:	Yeah, are there any other girls on your course?

Subject:	There's one other girl, there is one. I was quite surprised. She was quite surprised to see me as well but – and we get on quite well. We sort of stick together when they're all ganging up on us.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	I do, because there's a lady that I work with – down at control and some of the time she knows more than the engineers because she'll say well no, because it works for this and does this (yeah) so it can't work like that. And then they're like, oh yeah, hang on, better go and change that. And I just think seeing as there's a woman running this department, yet the men get all the credit for it. And I think a lot more women should go into it. I think it's just women are precise as well, and they've got attention to detail whereas sometimes a man will just go oh well, it's tough isn't it? It doesn't work, it doesn't work but yeah, I think definitely a lot more women should go for it.

Interviewer:	Why do you think they don't?

Subject:	I think it's just because it's so male dominated and women have just got a stereotypical image of can't be dirty, they can't be covered in grease and men have got to do all that and it's just the way things are, isn't it? And history.

Interviewer:	Do you think women need more information in school about what engineering really is?

Subject:	I think so. I speak to like loads of people and they say oh what do you do? And I tell 'em and they're like oh, I was going to do like plumbing in college, or I was gonna do electrics in college and I'm like well why didn't you? Because the boys took the mick out of me and I thought oh, it's quite sad really because you could see they really wanted to do it but they just didn't because of the way people reacted and I think it's just because you don't – like, I said, oh a picture of a mechanic on the front of the careers books is always a man, and I think if there was a man and a woman or one woman, then it would be different then because it's just the way people interpret things. I think we definitely need more information about it.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I dunno really. Hmm, I suppose it is nice to shock people. Like when they go what you doing then – you just waltz in here? No. But I can't really think of any disadvantages – er, sometimes people say really horrible stuff and you think well no, sorry we like that and it's just – I dunno, it's just the way people interpret it I think.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	I dunno because some of it, yeah, and then other times I just think no, because I thought it would be – the course itself would be a lot more practical but it's not that – there's only one subject that we do that we do any practical work in. And there's like two modules that I wouldn't generally associate with engineering, which is management and communication and I wouldn't have thought of doing them as part of an engineering course but they've turned out to be alright – I think I did quite well in them, so…

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course?

Subject:	Erm, the best thing I think was making off – we had to make a video and we could do anything we wanted and we did like why girls shouldn't walk home on their own, because I'm such a vulnerable looking female. I think the disadvantage would be the fact that it's not so practical (yeah).

Interviewer:	Are you glad, in that sense, that you are working (yeah) because you get that side to it, from work?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. I think that adds – that adds experience as well. If your course is practical, at least you can say well I've used this and I've made this whereas otherwise you just sort of – well I've talked about this and written an essay about this but never actually gone and done it (yeah) and I'm quite glad that I do work to be able to do that anyway.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you pleased that you chose this course then?

Subject:	Yeah, I am quite pleased that I did.

Interviewer:	OK and have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	I was last year. I was taught mechanics by a female lecturer and this year I was only taught Maths, I think.

Interviewer:	OK, have you noticed whether female lecturers have a different style of teaching or anything like that?

Subject:	Definitely. I found it, in some respects easier to learn from a female lecturer, but I'm – in others I found it harder to understand what she was trying to get across (yeah) and a lot of the male students thought that she wasn't a very good lecturer, but I actually thought she wasn't that bad, it was just the way she interpreted things (yeah) but it was different.

Interviewer:	Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	I think so, yeah. I think – again I think that it would encourage people – more girls anyway – if they could see that there was gonna be a female lecturer that's teaching them, then – that it wasn't just all men again (yeah) then I think it would definitely encourage them on – yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the lecturers treat the female and the male students the same? 

Subject:	Yeah, I think they do pretty much. I think – yeah, I think all our lecturers this year wouldn't have cared – they just saw the person (yeah) and they didn't – it was like well you know, you're not having an extra couple of days because you're a girl, or – and I think that was really good because they just got on with it. They didn't see you as a boy or a girl, they'd seen you as just who you are.

Interviewer:	OK, that's good. Is there anything or anyone, since you've started, that you'd say has been like the biggest influence on you?

Subject:	Probably just the four people that I work with in the office, at work, because like at least two have done the sort of – not had a degree or anything like that and they've come and they know so much just from doing what they're doing and I think, oh God, if they can do that without having a degree or anything and I – then what could I do if I've got this degree? And they are really encouraging, the amount of work they take on and yeah – I think the four people I work with in the office, at work, they are pretty encouraging.

Interviewer:	OK that's good. At Uni has the teaching that you've had involved much group work?

Subject:	Erm, we did – the video was one big group project and we had a management project that was a group one, but I think that's it really.

Interviewer:	Do you have to choose who you work with, or do you get put in groups when you're…

Subject:	We choose who we work with.

Interviewer:	Yeah. And do you prefer to work with men or women or aren't you bothered?

Subject:	I don't really mind whether it's male or female. I think I just go on the ones that I actually think are gonna do any work, rather than what sex they are (yeah) but the people I worked with this year, there was a few of them who did the foundation year with me, last year, so we already knew each other. So I worked with them because we knew how each other worked (yeah) and – yeah, I don't think I really see them as whether it's a boy or a girl, I just get on with it now if I think they're gonna do work.

Interviewer:	OK, have the group projects that you've done gone quite well?

Subject:	Yeah, I think the video we had about 70/80% in and the management project, I think we had about 60/65 in. So yeah, we've been quite good.

Interviewer:	Do you think that doing group work at Uni helps you in – in work, or not?

Subject:	I'm not sure because a lot of the time in work you have to be independent and just get on with it yourself, 'cos other people have got their own work to do. But then I think it's – it's good if you have a big project for the engineers that they all need to work together on, because then one can't boss the other one around and one's not better than the other one. I don't know, I think it works both ways so you know what to expect in a team, but you can work on your own as well. You take all your own aspect of your project and you… so I'm not sure really.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Have you used much of what you've learnt in the classroom in the workplace?

Subject:	Erm, some work calculations I've used in mechanics, I've used in work and a lot of other maths. But other than I really – I'm not – I don't really know – communication more than anything, how to put things across to people when you're talking to a supplier or a customer on the phone, but I'm not sure. I'll probably apply it more next year without thinking about it, and I probably just haven't noticed doing it.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think it works the other way – do you think things that you've learnt at work, help you make sense of…

Subject:	Yeah definitely. Yeah, definitely, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Can you tell me a bit about the company that you're working for? Like how big they are and what they do?

Subject:	They're called [name]. They started in a little garage and now they got I think it's three – about five different offices around Wales and England and they deal with hydraulics, pneumatics, tools, filters, compressers, pipe work – everything – a bit of everything really. Erm, they're one of the leading hydraulic dealers and got big contracts with [company] and the Millennium stadium and loads of different big companies, and I didn't even realise this company exists. Erm, it's like a family based company, erm – that's about it.

Interviewer:	Are there many women working for them?

Subject:	There's quite a few. There's another girl in the office with me and there's Leah, who I think you're going to meet in a bit (yeah) and – yeah, there is quite a few. It's mostly like admin jobs but we sort of also have a chance of purchasing new pumps or whatever, and dealing with orders that come in off customers and there is quite a few women working there.

Interviewer:	OK. Did you have a choice of companies to go to?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, I could either come up with a contact for a company and then [lecturer] and [administrator] would go in and talk to them or [lecturer] said he knew a few companies, and I thought well, I'll go for them being as he knows them because I'm not really in a position to go in and start poaching a place, and he said he knew about [company] and it's this lovely little company on this industrial estate and he knew [name], who's one of the Directors, and he just rang him up on a Tuesday and said oh, we've got someone who wants to come and work for you. And he says oh, OK, send her down on the Friday. It was all – just run from there then.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you think that that company would be good for you?

Subject:	Erm, I think because they were quite – well I thought, at the time, they were quite small (yeah) and they were local cos' I can't drive, and I just thought it would be interesting because I had never thought of – I had always thought, I think, of engineering as cars or big aeroplane engines and – and then I went down there and seen it's not all like that, there's other spectrums. 

Interviewer:	OK, have the University helped prepare you for being in the workplace at all?

Subject:	Erm, yes, [lecturer] and [administrator] were quite good, before I started last year. Erm, but I think a lot of it has come from just expecting the worse though. Erm, but it's not that bad. I think it has prepared me to an extent but I think I just had to prepare myself the rest of the way.

Interviewer:	What have the worst and the best things about the placement been so far?

Subject:	Erm, I think the worst thing was the first time I ever went out on site and I went to service a compressor and it was homed in a tiny, little room and I was literally sliding my way between it and it tripped out and made this really loud noise and I have never been so frightened in all my life but I've started to get used to it again now. Erm, and I think the best thing has been just going to all these different places and factories and seeing what they make and seeing how it's made, and probably the best place I've been is Avon Racing tyres, to do an air leak test and I spent two weeks there and it was awesome just watching tyres being made. It was something that I just couldn't believe that much went into it. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. That's interesting. How do you think that being at work differs to being at University?

Subject:	I can't stay in bed all day (laughs). It's just a lot more – I think it's prepared me for like getting out of bed a lot earlier, because I was – last year I think I was proper into staying in bed as late as possible, and now I've started to wake up about – if I'm going to work by about 9 O'clock anyway. So now I should be active. And I think it's just prepared me for the real world – I've seen, taken off my rose tinted glasses and seen things for how it is. So yeah, it's been quite good.

Interviewer:	Do you spend half the week in Uni and half at work?

Subject:	Yeah, I do two days in Uni and three days at work.

Interviewer:	So what happens through the summer do you just work?

Subject:	I work full time.

Interviewer:	Yeah – Ok do you think that the course and the work fit together quite well, or are they like two completely separate things really?

Subject:	They do fit together fairly well. Again some of it I can't see myself applying in work now and vice versa but probably next year and the year after, I'll do it and I won't even realise I'm doing it until I just stop and look back (yeah). So – I dunno, it's hard to say because there is like certain aspects that really do fit together really well and then there's others that are on a totally different planet (yeah) so I think next year I'll sort of find that out a bit more.

Interviewer:	OK, have you encountered any issues in the workplace that you think have been like because you are female?

Subject:	Erm, no not really – like everyone down at [company] has been like really good and encouraging and I wouldn't say anyone has said oh I'm not working with her because she's a girl. They have all been really nice. Sometimes I think I go out on site and people sort of look as if to say, oh that's a girl coming on site – you know? What's she doing here? And once I was told – I went to a Gatehouse in a company and the man behind the counter turned round to the engineer I was with and said sorry, we don't allow children on site and I was sort of taken back and I started laughing. I thought he was joking and he said ah, I thought, you know, are you gonna tell me you're about 25 or something. I said close. But other than that I think everyone's quite encouraging really. Nobody's sort of well, what you doing that for? And everyone's pretty good there.

Interviewer:	OK. In terms of your career then, what do you see yourself doing when you finish the course?

Subject:	Erm, I'm not really sure. I think I'd still like to go into the aerospace industry (yeah) because that's what I started with but I'm not sure how I want to go into it yet. Like I said, I'd like to set up my own business and build planes and have my own airline and service them, or – but I need money for that (yeah). But I don't know, I think I'd still like to go into aerospace but I don't know. I think I just have to see how I feel at the end of it. Like I said I wanted to move to Australia, so perhaps I could go and work for Air Quantas over there, or something, but no I'm not sure yet, I think I'm just gonna have to see how I feel when I finish.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you feel that the career prospects are good in mechanical engineering?

Subject:	I dunno, it seems to be getting better now, but it can just rise and fall so quickly (yeah). Erm, it is quite good, especially if you get a qualification to go with it but if you don't have that, you've just got to work really hard to get to it. So – I dunno, I think they are quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all like the career choices that you've made so far? (yeah) Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	Sometimes I do, when it's a cold, rainy morning and I'm out of bed and at 7 O'clock I do think, oh I wish I was just going to Uni today, but I don't ever seriously sit down and think oh why have I done this? Why am I doing this to myself? Because I think, at the end of the day, it's all going to be worth it, because I can walk into an interview and even if somebody next to me has got a better degree I've still got 5 years experience that they haven't got. So, yeah, I'm quite happy with everything I've done really.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Erm, help – unstable some times, erm, challenging (yeah), misunderstood, erm dirty...

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those things are like big problematic for you at all or…?

Subject:	I think the biggest one with me was because I misunderstood it. I thought it was just a narrow tunnel with cars and aeroplanes (yeah) and that was it really and then I sort of opened my eyes up and realised there was so much more to it (yeah) that I just didn't even realise and I think it is just a misunderstanding – people – I think that's why girls don't go into it, because they think oh cars, I don't want to fix cars (yeah) but it's not just fixing cars there's so much more to it. I think that's the main thing I've learned while I've worked in [company] here is there's so much more to engineering than just fixing cars.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the situation will get better for women in the industry, or…?

Subject:	I'd like to think so, because there's a lot more incentives now for women to go into it – a lot more companies are – want a woman to come and work for them because they look – it looks better doesn't it? You show the – the Equal Opportunities and I think it will get better (yeah). I think it should get better.

Interviewer:	OK, that's everything, thank you very much, that's been really helpful.

turns.text: Yeah, they're really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you ever consider going to another University or studying full-time then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the only other Uni's I really applied to was like [university 1] – two in [university 2], and [university 3] and [university 3] rejected me. I didn't like [university 1] and I wasn't that keen on – I liked [university 1] but I wasn't as keen on [university 1] as I was on coming here because I just thought, ah, it's closer – like if something goes wrong (yeah) but it's far enough that I could be on my own and grow up a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, did you do your foundation here as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that if the Network 75 thing hadn't been available you'd have done the course full time or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely I would have done it full time. Yeah, I think I definitely would have – I wouldn't have gone and looked for someone to employ me while I was work – er, studying. I don't think I even would have done a sandwich year or anything like that, so yeah, I probably would have just got my head down and done it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you decided to do engineering, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did, but I didn't realise how some people would react to it. Like, I've gone out on site, with the company I work for now (yeah) and even if I walk up to a gatehouse first, and there's a man behind me, they'll look over my head and talk to the man behind me (really?). And I didn't realise people will – I thought people would be encouraging but some people really put you down (yeah) and the way they act – they act totally different when I'm sitting in the canteen talking to them, than when I'm not. And I just think well why? There's nothing – it's not like the old days now. But I realised it was quite male dominated, it was just the way people reacted to it that scared me more than anything (yeah). I can remember going for my interview in [university 2], and they split you up from your parents and you've go on a bus and you have a tour and everything and I was on a bus – a 52 seater bus, with 40 other boys and not one person spoke to me, and I thought oh great, I've got this for the next 3 to 4 years. But I've just got used to it now and I think I've sort of – it's built my confidence to a certain extent because I'll just start talking to people whether they want to or not. Whether they're scared of me or not, I'll just start talking to them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, are there any other girls on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There's one other girl, there is one. I was quite surprised. She was quite surprised to see me as well but – and we get on quite well. We sort of stick together when they're all ganging up on us.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do, because there's a lady that I work with – down at control and some of the time she knows more than the engineers because she'll say well no, because it works for this and does this (yeah) so it can't work like that. And then they're like, oh yeah, hang on, better go and change that. And I just think seeing as there's a woman running this department, yet the men get all the credit for it. And I think a lot more women should go into it. I think it's just women are precise as well, and they've got attention to detail whereas sometimes a man will just go oh well, it's tough isn't it? It doesn't work, it doesn't work but yeah, I think definitely a lot more women should go for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think they don't?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it's just because it's so male dominated and women have just got a stereotypical image of can't be dirty, they can't be covered in grease and men have got to do all that and it's just the way things are, isn't it? And history.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think women need more information in school about what engineering really is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. I speak to like loads of people and they say oh what do you do? And I tell 'em and they're like oh, I was going to do like plumbing in college, or I was gonna do electrics in college and I'm like well why didn't you? Because the boys took the mick out of me and I thought oh, it's quite sad really because you could see they really wanted to do it but they just didn't because of the way people reacted and I think it's just because you don't – like, I said, oh a picture of a mechanic on the front of the careers books is always a man, and I think if there was a man and a woman or one woman, then it would be different then because it's just the way people interpret things. I think we definitely need more information about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I dunno really. Hmm, I suppose it is nice to shock people. Like when they go what you doing then – you just waltz in here? No. But I can't really think of any disadvantages – er, sometimes people say really horrible stuff and you think well no, sorry we like that and it's just – I dunno, it's just the way people interpret it I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I dunno because some of it, yeah, and then other times I just think no, because I thought it would be – the course itself would be a lot more practical but it's not that – there's only one subject that we do that we do any practical work in. And there's like two modules that I wouldn't generally associate with engineering, which is management and communication and I wouldn't have thought of doing them as part of an engineering course but they've turned out to be alright – I think I did quite well in them, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best thing I think was making off – we had to make a video and we could do anything we wanted and we did like why girls shouldn't walk home on their own, because I'm such a vulnerable looking female. I think the disadvantage would be the fact that it's not so practical (yeah).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you glad, in that sense, that you are working (yeah) because you get that side to it, from work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. I think that adds – that adds experience as well. If your course is practical, at least you can say well I've used this and I've made this whereas otherwise you just sort of – well I've talked about this and written an essay about this but never actually gone and done it (yeah) and I'm quite glad that I do work to be able to do that anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you pleased that you chose this course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I am quite pleased that I did.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK and have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was last year. I was taught mechanics by a female lecturer and this year I was only taught Maths, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you noticed whether female lecturers have a different style of teaching or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. I found it, in some respects easier to learn from a female lecturer, but I'm – in others I found it harder to understand what she was trying to get across (yeah) and a lot of the male students thought that she wasn't a very good lecturer, but I actually thought she wasn't that bad, it was just the way she interpreted things (yeah) but it was different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, yeah. I think – again I think that it would encourage people – more girls anyway – if they could see that there was gonna be a female lecturer that's teaching them, then – that it wasn't just all men again (yeah) then I think it would definitely encourage them on – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the lecturers treat the female and the male students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think they do pretty much. I think – yeah, I think all our lecturers this year wouldn't have cared – they just saw the person (yeah) and they didn't – it was like well you know, you're not having an extra couple of days because you're a girl, or – and I think that was really good because they just got on with it. They didn't see you as a boy or a girl, they'd seen you as just who you are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's good. Is there anything or anyone, since you've started, that you'd say has been like the biggest influence on you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably just the four people that I work with in the office, at work, because like at least two have done the sort of – not had a degree or anything like that and they've come and they know so much just from doing what they're doing and I think, oh God, if they can do that without having a degree or anything and I – then what could I do if I've got this degree? And they are really encouraging, the amount of work they take on and yeah – I think the four people I work with in the office, at work, they are pretty encouraging.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that's good. At Uni has the teaching that you've had involved much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, we did – the video was one big group project and we had a management project that was a group one, but I think that's it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to choose who you work with, or do you get put in groups when you're…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We choose who we work with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. And do you prefer to work with men or women or aren't you bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't really mind whether it's male or female. I think I just go on the ones that I actually think are gonna do any work, rather than what sex they are (yeah) but the people I worked with this year, there was a few of them who did the foundation year with me, last year, so we already knew each other. So I worked with them because we knew how each other worked (yeah) and – yeah, I don't think I really see them as whether it's a boy or a girl, I just get on with it now if I think they're gonna do work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have the group projects that you've done gone quite well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think the video we had about 70/80% in and the management project, I think we had about 60/65 in. So yeah, we've been quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that doing group work at Uni helps you in – in work, or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm not sure because a lot of the time in work you have to be independent and just get on with it yourself, 'cos other people have got their own work to do. But then I think it's – it's good if you have a big project for the engineers that they all need to work together on, because then one can't boss the other one around and one's not better than the other one. I don't know, I think it works both ways so you know what to expect in a team, but you can work on your own as well. You take all your own aspect of your project and you… so I'm not sure really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. Have you used much of what you've learnt in the classroom in the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, some work calculations I've used in mechanics, I've used in work and a lot of other maths. But other than I really – I'm not – I don't really know – communication more than anything, how to put things across to people when you're talking to a supplier or a customer on the phone, but I'm not sure. I'll probably apply it more next year without thinking about it, and I probably just haven't noticed doing it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think it works the other way – do you think things that you've learnt at work, help you make sense of…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah definitely. Yeah, definitely, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Can you tell me a bit about the company that you're working for? Like how big they are and what they do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They're called [name]. They started in a little garage and now they got I think it's three – about five different offices around Wales and England and they deal with hydraulics, pneumatics, tools, filters, compressers, pipe work – everything – a bit of everything really. Erm, they're one of the leading hydraulic dealers and got big contracts with [company] and the Millennium stadium and loads of different big companies, and I didn't even realise this company exists. Erm, it's like a family based company, erm – that's about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there many women working for them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There's quite a few. There's another girl in the office with me and there's Leah, who I think you're going to meet in a bit (yeah) and – yeah, there is quite a few. It's mostly like admin jobs but we sort of also have a chance of purchasing new pumps or whatever, and dealing with orders that come in off customers and there is quite a few women working there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Did you have a choice of companies to go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, I could either come up with a contact for a company and then [lecturer] and [administrator] would go in and talk to them or [lecturer] said he knew a few companies, and I thought well, I'll go for them being as he knows them because I'm not really in a position to go in and start poaching a place, and he said he knew about [company] and it's this lovely little company on this industrial estate and he knew [name], who's one of the Directors, and he just rang him up on a Tuesday and said oh, we've got someone who wants to come and work for you. And he says oh, OK, send her down on the Friday. It was all – just run from there then.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you think that that company would be good for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think because they were quite – well I thought, at the time, they were quite small (yeah) and they were local cos' I can't drive, and I just thought it would be interesting because I had never thought of – I had always thought, I think, of engineering as cars or big aeroplane engines and – and then I went down there and seen it's not all like that, there's other spectrums.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have the University helped prepare you for being in the workplace at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes, [lecturer] and [administrator] were quite good, before I started last year. Erm, but I think a lot of it has come from just expecting the worse though. Erm, but it's not that bad. I think it has prepared me to an extent but I think I just had to prepare myself the rest of the way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What have the worst and the best things about the placement been so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think the worst thing was the first time I ever went out on site and I went to service a compressor and it was homed in a tiny, little room and I was literally sliding my way between it and it tripped out and made this really loud noise and I have never been so frightened in all my life but I've started to get used to it again now. Erm, and I think the best thing has been just going to all these different places and factories and seeing what they make and seeing how it's made, and probably the best place I've been is Avon Racing tyres, to do an air leak test and I spent two weeks there and it was awesome just watching tyres being made. It was something that I just couldn't believe that much went into it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. That's interesting. How do you think that being at work differs to being at University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I can't stay in bed all day (laughs). It's just a lot more – I think it's prepared me for like getting out of bed a lot earlier, because I was – last year I think I was proper into staying in bed as late as possible, and now I've started to wake up about – if I'm going to work by about 9 O'clock anyway. So now I should be active. And I think it's just prepared me for the real world – I've seen, taken off my rose tinted glasses and seen things for how it is. So yeah, it's been quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you spend half the week in Uni and half at work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I do two days in Uni and three days at work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what happens through the summer do you just work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I work full time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – Ok do you think that the course and the work fit together quite well, or are they like two completely separate things really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They do fit together fairly well. Again some of it I can't see myself applying in work now and vice versa but probably next year and the year after, I'll do it and I won't even realise I'm doing it until I just stop and look back (yeah). So – I dunno, it's hard to say because there is like certain aspects that really do fit together really well and then there's others that are on a totally different planet (yeah) so I think next year I'll sort of find that out a bit more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you encountered any issues in the workplace that you think have been like because you are female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no not really – like everyone down at [company] has been like really good and encouraging and I wouldn't say anyone has said oh I'm not working with her because she's a girl. They have all been really nice. Sometimes I think I go out on site and people sort of look as if to say, oh that's a girl coming on site – you know? What's she doing here? And once I was told – I went to a Gatehouse in a company and the man behind the counter turned round to the engineer I was with and said sorry, we don't allow children on site and I was sort of taken back and I started laughing. I thought he was joking and he said ah, I thought, you know, are you gonna tell me you're about 25 or something. I said close. But other than that I think everyone's quite encouraging really. Nobody's sort of well, what you doing that for? And everyone's pretty good there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. In terms of your career then, what do you see yourself doing when you finish the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm not really sure. I think I'd still like to go into the aerospace industry (yeah) because that's what I started with but I'm not sure how I want to go into it yet. Like I said, I'd like to set up my own business and build planes and have my own airline and service them, or – but I need money for that (yeah). But I don't know, I think I'd still like to go into aerospace but I don't know. I think I just have to see how I feel at the end of it. Like I said I wanted to move to Australia, so perhaps I could go and work for Air Quantas over there, or something, but no I'm not sure yet, I think I'm just gonna have to see how I feel when I finish.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you feel that the career prospects are good in mechanical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I dunno, it seems to be getting better now, but it can just rise and fall so quickly (yeah). Erm, it is quite good, especially if you get a qualification to go with it but if you don't have that, you've just got to work really hard to get to it. So – I dunno, I think they are quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all like the career choices that you've made so far? (yeah) Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sometimes I do, when it's a cold, rainy morning and I'm out of bed and at 7 O'clock I do think, oh I wish I was just going to Uni today, but I don't ever seriously sit down and think oh why have I done this? Why am I doing this to myself? Because I think, at the end of the day, it's all going to be worth it, because I can walk into an interview and even if somebody next to me has got a better degree I've still got 5 years experience that they haven't got. So, yeah, I'm quite happy with everything I've done really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, help – unstable some times, erm, challenging (yeah), misunderstood, erm dirty...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those things are like big problematic for you at all or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the biggest one with me was because I misunderstood it. I thought it was just a narrow tunnel with cars and aeroplanes (yeah) and that was it really and then I sort of opened my eyes up and realised there was so much more to it (yeah) that I just didn't even realise and I think it is just a misunderstanding – people – I think that's why girls don't go into it, because they think oh cars, I don't want to fix cars (yeah) but it's not just fixing cars there's so much more to it. I think that's the main thing I've learned while I've worked in [company] here is there's so much more to engineering than just fixing cars.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the situation will get better for women in the industry, or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd like to think so, because there's a lot more incentives now for women to go into it – a lot more companies are – want a woman to come and work for them because they look – it looks better doesn't it? You show the – the Equal Opportunities and I think it will get better (yeah). I think it should get better.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's everything, thank you very much, that's been really helpful.
